title: Notes of Ministry - 4 - March 1973

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 4 - March 1973 (2028)/Notes of Ministry - 4 - March 1 - Various.epub

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: What is in mind is the securing of a sanctified company, perhaps we might say, a company of sanctified ones. The height of the truth is in the last scripture read, but I thought we might see the divine road to it. It is not just a matter of light—“for both he that sanctifies and those sanctified are all of one”—but of spiritual experience. Our hymn (No. 104) contained references to the Lord’s reproach and suffering, and I thought we would begin there. I think we would recognise! that the principle of separation, whilst basic to any right position according to God, is not necessarily an end in itself, but is in view of something else.

What links these scriptures together is the truth of sanctification, an expression used in 2 Timothy 2—a sanctified vessel meet for the Master’s use. That is more the external, of owning the Lord’s name and departing from iniquity, which is an essential thing at the present time. But I chose the Hebrews 13 scripture because it is personal to Christ. It is not just a matter of principles, though it involves principles, but you go out to a Person. What is more, whilst we have to dwell a good deal on going without the camp, what really provides the basis is the blood that is taken into the presence of God; then the body is burned outside the camp. But first, the blood is taken in.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: Am I right in thinking that that was on the day of atonement?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes; it is the basis of all blessing, the basis not only of righteousness, but of holiness, for God has been propitiated in regard of sin.

paragraphs.speaker: FCM
text: Is that the blood in relation to the purpose and counsel of God to have men in His presence?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right; and to have them there in holiness. The first thing is to get a sense that every holy claim of God involved in the incoming of sin is met by the blood that is taken into His immediate presence. I think we shall see the value of that later in our enquiry. It says that of those beasts whose blood is taken in, the bodies were burned outside the camp.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: In his first epistle John refers not only to the blood but to the Person. He says of Him, “He is the propitiation for our sins, but not for ours alone, but also for the whole world”.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: So there is a very wide and extensive basis that God has established in the blood being taken in to His immediate presence, in the type.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: Does that mean that, whatever happens here below, His glory is met?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes, and it includes not just the sins or the state of persons, but God being given a righteous basis to continue with a collective testimony here, because it stands over against

“the camp”. The camp, according to the Hebrews setting, is the religious profession, which perhaps we do not feel sufficiently, the dishonour to God at the present time in what outwardly professes His name.

paragraphs.speaker: BES
text: In Leviticus 4 it is in connection with the sin of the priest, or of the whole congregation, that the blood was carried in. In the case of the prince or the common person it was not. Does that connect with what you have been saying?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes; because I think it is the priestly company that is in mind; it is with those who presume to draw near to God that the greatest sin has occurred, as with the two sons of Aaron. The sanctification is by His own blood, and gives God a warrant for going forward with His original intention to have a sanctified company here on earth. There is an immediate connection with the Sanctifier, according to chapter two, an order of humanity that is after Christ

paragraphs.speaker: PNS
text: Does the immediate connection between the blood and the holy of holies, both in this chapter and in chapter ten, underline what you are saying as to holiness being requisite for the service of God?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is the comparison with 2 Timothy 2, so often quoted in recent years, and this chapter which emphasizes holiness, and holiness enters into sanctification. It is a question of our being committed wholly to God.

paragraphs.speaker: AAB
text: It says in Revelation 22, “He that is holy, let him be sanctified still”. There is a fixed condition of things contemplated in that passage. Mr. Taylor used to speak of it, suggesting that we are in that time now.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I am glad you recall that. He said it is fixed, for good or for evil; “Let the filthy make himself filthy still … and he that is holy, let him be sanctified still”. It is a question of the character of the service that is to be rendered to God in a day when the love of the most grows cold. The profession itself is a perversion of the truth.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Could you say something as to what distinction there might be between being sanctified by the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, and sanctifying the people by His own blood, and whether those two things together would not bring the Supper into our mind.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is exactly what is in my mind, because it links the two chapters; both enter into the Supper. Do you think the Supper in that respect is the means by which practical sanctification is sustained amongst the saints?

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Would it provide weekly a point to which we rally as the sanctified company? It is not that these two scriptures refer directly to the Supper, but the references to the offering of His body, and “by his own blood”, would immediately remind us of the loaf and the cup, would they not?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is my thought in suggesting these scriptures, which, I think, shows that the Spirit of God is with us now in seeking to get at this immense truth, that God is after a company of sanctified persons. I think it settles the question of whether we should use the term “position”. Those who go outside the camp, and accept the reproach of the Christ, are on the way to sanctification. I doubt whether there is any real sanctification apart from accepting the reproach of Christ; and that is not just in the world as such. The slander and misrepresentation that has occurred recently makes you feel increasingly the departure of those who profess, in which we have to own our part. But the blood going in is the assurance that God has the answer to every moral question.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: I am sure that is right. The blood is sprinkled around the altar, before the altar, and so on. I wondered whether “sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ”

extended our minds to the bodies that were burned outside the camp. There is more in it than that, but wondered if it linked with the reference in chapter 13 to the bodies, the allusion being to something in relation to the death of Christ. I wondered whether the scriptures do not link together, as if the apostle in writing had been drawing on the same sources all the way through.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right. He starts with God’s highest thoughts. In the Corinthians Paul starts with God’s highest thoughts, but the way we approach the truth is delineated afterwards.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: There is an element of reproach in connection with the bodies that were burned outside the camp. I am wondering how it bears on what Mr. B. was just saying.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I think it involves a full committal to the position of reproach. I do not think we shall escape reproach until the Lord comes. If we do, I think it will mean we have not taken our position here in relation to Him who suffered outside the gate.

paragraphs.speaker: EOPM
text: Does this link at all with what we were considering on Lord’s day afternoon in 1 Corinthians; the presentation there of the Supper, the emphasis on the body and the blood, but “in the night in which he was delivered up”?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I think there is a link. What I am concerned about in this particular setting is, “therefore let us go forth to him”. However broken the day, however great the unfaithfulness among those who confess His name, you can still take up this position, you go forth to Him without the camp.

paragraphs.speaker: BWW
text: A little earlier in this chapter His unchangingness is emphasized. It is the same Person all the way through.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: The Person is the same. What God is at is not just to indicate our course in any difficulty that may arise, but to go out to Him without the camp, bearing His reproach. We have to make sure that the reproach is not on our account, because the way we act at times is not in accordance with the truth we supposedly hold, or stand for; but, nevertheless, the fact is that it is the reproach of Christ that is upon those who are seeking to pursue the truth at the present time.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: Paul speaks about the scandal of the cross. Is that a similar thought? He boasts in it, does he not?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: He does.

paragraphs.speaker: RET
text: The life being in the blood, does that give the basis of God maintaining His righteousness?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: And His holiness—sanctification involves holiness as well as righteousness. But it is “to him”. The Lord is still the gathering point and I think we want to be sure that, after the usurpation that we had to suffer for so long, the Lord is still the gathering Centre. We go out to Him, bearing His reproach. It is outside “the camp”, an organised system of things that professedly owns him, but in fact denies Him.

paragraphs.speaker: AJE
text: You were speaking about a collective position. There are two references to “us” in this portion we read; scripture confirms that there is that. There are some that we walked with recently who strenuously affirm that everything is individual. We have to take the position one by one, but we find company, that is “us” and “we”.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is outside the camp, and that comes very close home. We can condemn the blatant errors that there are in the established systems, but “outside the camp”, I think, involves anything that has been an affront to the declaration of God in the blood and the body of our Lord. He suffered without the gate, and “we have not here an abiding city, but we seek the coming one. By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise continually to God”—that is, the service of God is in mind.

paragraphs.speaker: FCM
text: It seems that there is a continuity—it is the same Person to whom we go out by whom this continual service of praise is maintained, in that position.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is so, and I think the Supper has a very great part in this. When we break bread we do so in the wilderness, and the wilderness supposes the acceptance of the reproach of the Christ. But, inwardly, it involves being in touch with One who ever was, and ever will be what He was, God over all, blessed for ever. There was a time when One said to Another, “Thou hast prepared me a body”. The spirit of revelation is in Paul’s quoting Psalm 40. David seems to rise to a type of Christ. The veil is drawn aside as to what transpired between the One that we know now as the Father, and the Other, the Son. It illustrates what Mr. Darby says, that we do not speak of divine Persons as having the same mind or the same will; it is one will, but several willings.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: The Lord speaks of Himself, when He was here, as meek and lowly in heart. We often speak about being humble—we appreciate the need of it more than ever—but the bearing of the reproach would produce that.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right. The only safe attitude is not to assume to any position; the Lord is the gathering Centre, and we are to go outside the camp, whatever that may involve, and seek Him. What do we come out to? A system of rules again? An enlightened view of what separation means?—though we need that, too. The centre, it seems to me, is that you go out to a Person and you accept His reproach; and that same Person, as Mr. M. has said, is the One who is the Leader of the praises, as Hebrews 2 shows.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: It is not only that it is the same Person. It is the same Person in the same position publicly. It is still so. That is to say, the sacrifice of praise offered continually to God by Him is not done inside the camp.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I hope the brethren have got the significance of that remark, because immediately we speak of any official position we have lost the real meaning of the scripture.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Yes, I think it is essential that we should be continually reminded that we go forth to Him; but the reproach in this section is not, for instance, the same as in the last chapter of Galatians, is it?—where Paul glories in the cross and he is crucified to the world, and the world to him. This is reproach from the public profession—not reproach from the world.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is exactly what is in my mind.

paragraphs.speaker: DER
text: So Peter says, “If ye are reproached in the name of Christ, blessed are ye”; it is in the name, not for the name.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Well, it is a great thing to have the sense that the Lord is still the gathering Centre. If we have got that clear, we can go to chapter 10 and see that what lies behind this is that, “coming into the world”, that is, with that in view, the Lord said, “Thou tookest no pleasure in burnt-offerings and sacrifices for sins. Then I said, Lo, I come (in the roll of the book it is written of me) to do, O God, thy will”. It is a question of a body prepared for Him—“Thou has prepared me a body”.

The writer of this epistle could give a spiritual meaning to what is written in the psalm, which was doubtless the result of David’s experiences. Paul, as we assume, puts his own interpretation on it, not just “ears hast thou digged”, but, “Thou hast prepared me a body”.

References to both the body and the blood being brought together at the Supper, link us with the occasion that sustains us in the sense that the Lord is the gathering Centre. But what lies behind it is the mystery of the incarnation. I expect that is why the Lord said, through ministry, that in relation to the cup the element of worship should enter into our thanksgiving.
Who was it who filled out the will of God here?

paragraphs.speaker: AAB
text: Peter addresses the saints as “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, by sanctification of the Spirit, unto the obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”. Do we have there another veiled allusion to the truth of the Supper? “The obedience” is connected with what was effected in His body. One was feeling the need of getting to what lies behind the externals. It is that which is going to hold our hearts in fidelity, is it not?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I believe so, and the sanctification of the worshipper is a settled matter in this chapter—it is established in perpetuity. It is contrasted with the worshipper approaching, and then the high priest dies, the thing is not continuous; but now the position of the sanctified is a settled matter; it is established according to the will of God. But behind it was the mind of One of the Persons of the Godhead to come—“Lo, I come”.

paragraphs.speaker: AAB
text: We need to appropriate this more, “This is my body, which is for you”. It has in view that we appropriate the spiritual side of this matter. It would build up a constitution to stand in the testimony.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: It seems that the Supper is the great occasion for sustaining the saints in this, because it is a time of feeding upon Christ, for seeing what was, and is, in Him; and I think the mystery of the incarnation comes into it. This scripture is, we might say, a conversation between two of Them; One willing to come, and the Other preparing a body for Him, and that was the body in which the Lord was found, and in which the will of God was filled out perfectly, so, “By which will we have been sanctified”.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: So the sanctification by the offering of the body reflects the blessedness and the holiness of the body, “Thou hast prepared me a body”.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes; then the fixity of that acceptance, before God, is an established matter. It can never be broken into because the One who gave His body has settled the matter once and for all.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: How much more liberty we should have if we understood that! Why is it that we do not take it in?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Perhaps we do not give ourselves sufficient time for contemplation. I think we rely on knowledge, which is limited anyway with many of us; but we are to contemplate this Person, who could say before the incarnation, “I come to do, O God, thy will”, and in Gethsemane He says to His Father, “Not my will, but thine be done” (Luke 22: 42). It is submission, subjection, and devotion in perfection in a Man. Who is He who could declare God? This enters into the cup, I believe. There is a depth and fulness in the cup that involves what we have said—the apprehension at least that the One who came to fill out the will of God is none less than God Himself, but in manhood.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Do you think that some of our insufficiency in the service of God may relate to our stopping at no longer having any conscience of sins, but that sanctification is something that is then positively entered into and provides a basis for entering fully into the service of God in the sanctified company?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is good. That is what we have here, no more remembrance of sin. It does not say, ‘no more consciousness of sin’, but, “no longer any conscience of sins”. That is, the conscience is clear by this wondrous sacrifice, so that we approach in the liberty that has been established in the giving of the body of Christ.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: I think Mr. Stoney has things to say on the point that if we are just occupied with the fact that our sins are forgiven even occupied with the fact that we have no longer conscience of sins—we may not proceed very far in the service of God. What is needed is the additional sense of what it is that He has achieved through sanctification—so that He has secured the praises of God in a company who have, if we may say so, left the question of sins behind. They are now on ground that does not include it.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right.

paragraphs.speaker: AAB
text: To extend what Mr. B. was saying as to the additional thought in Hebrews 10 of the burnt-offering, you referred a moment ago to our acceptance, and the liberating power of that in our souls in the service of God. That is connected with our apprehension of the burnt-offering. I was thinking of the stupendous character of the thought of the will of God, but the Lord Jesus provided everything that was called for in connection with the will of God; going beyond the meeting of the exigency that had arisen through the incoming of sin, to the establishment of every divine purpose.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right; and that enters into the cup, does it not?

paragraphs.speaker: RET
text: I wondered if it would be right to hold in our minds the distinctiveness of the loaf, speaking of the body, but yet holding the cup in a distinctive way too, the will of God in the body, but the liberating power that the cup should bring in. Would that be right?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I think so. The cup relates to what the Lord accomplished for God particularly, but the effects of it are still, according to 1 Corinthians 11, “for you”. What is effected for God liberates Him to come out in the fulness of what is in His own mind.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Does not that remark amplify for us the significance of the new covenant, attached to the cup? I was thinking of what you were saying, that it would be the thought of God’s disposition towards us. God is free to make Himself known in the personal way in which He has revealed Himself, and His whole disposition is known to us in that. We understand the new covenant in the cup.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: And we are not thinking of the new covenant as a matter of terms, but we come to the Ark of the covenant at the Supper; the One who is the Fulfiller of every thought of God; the fulness of it is there. It extends, of course, as the service proceeds. But it seems to me that it brings a liberating effect; for God anyway, and it should be for us. We are moving towards the understanding that God has sanctified ones, according to His will.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: So in that way the Supper becomes a fresh invitation to take that ground of being sanctified for His service; and it practically leads to that.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes, it does.

paragraphs.speaker: WJRB
text: I was thinking that Moses in Deuteronomy, when he places the covenant in the ark, says, “There they are”—it is fixed.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: We have come by means of Christ as the Ark of the covenant to the God who covenanted. It seems to me a most liberating thing that it was in God’s will that we should be sanctified, “by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”. That sacrifice has not to be repeated, so the position from God’s side is established. Whether it is so from our side would be a question of our apprehension of it.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: It is most important, what you are stressing now, because if there is any failure with us individually, we tend to forget this and our liberty is hindered.

paragraphs.speaker: FCM
text: In Chapter 8, in connection with the covenant, one of the effects is that “all shall know me in themselves”.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes, “in themselves”, so that the brother who gives thanks for the memorials is not just moved in his mind, but in his spirit, because it is a spiritual matter to understand that “by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”. There is no break in that. If we could see the position from God’s side I think it would help greatly in liberating us, because we so often take a subjective view and are limited according to the state. But we are to rise above that to what is established in God’s sight, that it is in His will that we should be set apart. It is not separated from; it is sanctified to something. We are committed to the service of the blessed God.

paragraphs.speaker: HRB
text: The Lord says, “For where two or three are gathered together unto my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18: 20).

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right; that would bear upon administration. What I am trying to get, for myself anyway, is this great thought of sanctification. All that the saints have passed through, the sorrow and the distress, should have had a separating effect from what is unholy, not only from what is not right. Now that in itself has a sanctifying effect. But there is a divine basis, “the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”. God is not going back on that, and we are to be liberated in our spirits to proceed with the remainder of the service at the Supper.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Would it be right to think that sanctification has a dignifying effect? It has been in my mind lately as to whether our exercises as to separation that have been pursued have altogether had that effect. My impression is that a christian is a person who moves with dignity. I think sanctification should have that effect, so that, while what we are saying bears directly on the service of God, sanctification has an effect all through the week.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I have no doubt it has. That leads really to our last scripture in Hebrews 2, “He that sanctifies and those sanctified are all of one”. There is a dignity about that, because it is an order of things that is patterned after Christ. There is no discrepancy between the Sanctifier and the sanctified. It is a dignified position, so that we can be before God in suitability, so that the Lord can take occasion, by the place He has amongst us, to hymn His God.

paragraphs.speaker: PC
text: So it would be the Sanctifier we should follow, and as following Him we surely will be, by being occupied with Him, sanctified persons. Our sensibilities increase all the time.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Occupation with Him who has established everything for God has a most sanctifying effect, it seems to me; as Mr. B. said it is the dignity of our position—that is really what is in this passage. How it was accomplished is not so much the point. It is predicated of certain persons that they are sanctified ones.

paragraphs.speaker: AAB
text: Does John 17 have a bearing on this? The Lord ennobles His, own there. “The glory which thou hast given me I have given them that they may be one” (John 17: 22). Then as to the daily matter, He speaks to the Father of sanctification, and then of sending His own into the world, as the Father had sent Him into the world.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: And in that section of John 17 He addresses the Father as “holy”, “Holy Father”.

Later on, when it is a question of God’s selection of certain ones, it is “Righteous Father”; He is perfectly righteous in what He has done in His selection. But when it is a question of their being preserved from the world He says, “Holy Father”. That bears upon this. What Mr. B. says has confirmed in my mind that it is the dignity of the sanctified ones; they are available now to Christ in relation to the service of God, “In the midst of the assembly will I sing thy praises”.

paragraphs.speaker: RET
text: J.T. said in Newcastle as to that reference to “Holy Father”, it was only the Lord who could say that and understand what He was saying.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Oh; surely! it is recorded for us. I have often wondered about the way things are recorded. Think of the Spirit of God recalling through John this prayer for us today, nearly 2,000 years later.

paragraphs.speaker: FCM
text: Does John 17 lead on to John 20, “My Father and your Father”. Is that the sanctified company?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right. It is the dignity that we arrive at, and arrive at, I think, realistically; that the Sanctifier and the sanctified are all of one. That is, the Lord has a company now serviceable to Him as He takes over in the service of God.

paragraphs.speaker: DER
text: It is wonderfully liberating that we are of the same order, stock, and lineage as Christ Himself; that He the Sanctifier, and we the sanctified, are all of one.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes. It is the order of humanity.

paragraphs.speaker: GWB
text: Would it be illustrated, in part at least, by Aaron’s sons and their father’s service? Of course, the antitype is much greater, but it is very impressive to view them as they are presented in the scripture. The dignity that has been referred to was certainly theirs as well as his.

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: Yes, indeed.

paragraphs.speaker: FNS
text: If we carry forward the truth and the reality of the Person who gave effect to the will of God would it not give us a sense of the dignity of the whole order of things, and that He has the place in the midst of such an assembly as this?
Would it not help to keep in our minds the dignity and the glory of all that God had in His thoughts, that has been established in this way?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: That is right. That is what has been in my mind in suggesting this line of truth, that it might promote with us a sense of what God has established in one blessed Man, and that Man is God. To me, that enters into our apprehension. We speak of the mystery of the incarnation, and of course it is; we cannot penetrate into One who, for instance, in John 3: 13, could say, “The Son of Man who is in heaven”. You just bow in worship.

paragraphs.speaker: ECB
text: Both these expressions, “those sanctified” and “the assembly” here, would be all-embracing, would they not? But then is it not a question of who is ready to be available?

paragraphs.speaker: CH
text: I think that is the point, and the way to it is in chapter 13, it seems to me. It is for all. The truth is all-embracing; it includes all saints in the mind of God. But it is a question of our arrival at it, and that is in the acceptance of the reproach of Christ, and as to anything connected with “the camp”, we are not having to do with it.

Barnet
13th January 1973

articles.title: THE COMFORT OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
articles.author: W. McKay

paragraphs.text: I want to speak of what is said here in Acts 9 “The assemblies... were increased through the comfort of the Holy Spirit”. I feel the time has come to experience this in an increasing way.

It is in John’s gospel that the Spirit is referred to as the Comforter. That is a very significant fact. It means that the Spirit should be known in that character in the last days, because John is writing in view of the last days. I do not mean to say that it has not applied to the presence of the Holy Spirit right through—it certainly has—but the fact that John is the only writer who refers to the Holy Spirit under that designation would suggest that as we are near to the end and get to the close of things, that particular service of the Holy Spirit will come into evidence in a greater way. So that, dear brethren, I think we need to know as together what the comfort of the Holy Spirit really is.

There is another feature attached to it in this verse, and that is the fear of the Lord. It says, “The assemblies throughout the whole of Judaea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, being edified and walking in the fear of the Lord, and were increased through the comfort of the Holy Spirit”. It is a very remarkable thing that the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit should be brought together in this one verse.

I feel, dear brethren, that the fear of the Lord is a very important feature at the present time. In the world around us it is almost completely set aside. Older brethren, who can go back 40 or 50 years, would tell us that the fear of God was more prevalent then, but things are reaching such a state in the world that it is now almost unknown—and not only in the world as such, but in professing christian bodies around us. Even much of what has happened amongst ourselves has shown a lack in this very feature. It is a very humbling matter that in our own experience we have seen persons who professed to be in relation to God but who have been marked by anything but the fear of God. It is a very, very solemn thing that. I believe that what God is looking for is the recovery of this feature amongst the saints at the close of the dispensation.

You will remember that it is in the book of Malachi, that is, the last book in the Old Testament, that we are told that “they that feared Jehovah spoke often one to another; and Jehovah observed it, and heard, and a book of remembrance was written ... And they shall be unto me a peculiar treasure” (Malachi 3: 16, 17). It shows the great value God places upon this feature. It is something to be thought about. “They shall be unto me a peculiar treasure … in the day that I prepare”. That is at the close of that dispensation. “They that feared Jehovah spoke often one to another”; it is not those that made profession, or those who could say great things, but those that feared Jehovah. What characterised the closing moments of the dispensation was peculiarly the fear of God.

Peter says, “If ye invoke as Father him who, without regard of persons, judges according to the work of each, pass your time of sojourn in fear” (1 Peter 1: 17). Peter had the truth of the kingdom, and he is stressing that side. He says, “Pass the time of your sojourn in fear, knowing that ye have been redeemed, not by corruptible things, as silver or gold, from your vain conversation”. So that the fear of God is to mark us. You will remember, too, that Joseph in his dealings with his brethren said, “I fear God” (Genesis 42: 18). This feature is very important, and what gives it more importance than anything else is the fact that it characterised the Lord Jesus in His holy manhood here. Perhaps you had not thought of that, but it is an amazing fact that He who had equal part in the Deity with the Father and the Spirit, as here in manhood was marked in His humanity by the fear of God. That is a remarkable thing. Hebrews 5 tells us that in the days of His flesh He “offered up both supplications and entreaties to him who was able to save him out of death, with strong crying and tears” (Hebrews 5: 7). The Lord Jesus felt all that was coming upon Him in regard to His death and the sin question, the forsaking of God—how the Lord felt that! And then the scripture in Hebrews tells us that He was heard in that He feared. Surely it is deeply affecting to think of that.

Now that gives this feature a value that nothing else could. The Lord Jesus was perfect in it. He was the Leader in it, as in everything else; but we have to learn from that and take on this matter of the fear of God.

So in this section of the book of the Acts these beloved brethren had been through much. They had seen the way God had acted in relation to Ananias and Sapphira, and the result was that the fear of God was with them. They had seen the way God had allowed Stephen to be put to death, and James to be put to death; and they saw the way that the Lord came out to deal with Saul of Tarsus. The result was that they were walking in the fear of the Lord. O, dear brethren, I would like to press that; it is so important—“the fear of the Lord”, and then “the comfort of the Holy Spirit”. I think the two go together.

I have the impression that the comfort of the Holy Spirit comes to us in the ministry. I am not overlooking in any sense the actual presence here of the Holy Spirit, and that He can convey to any individual saint, at any time, a sense of comfort and encouragement. I am not overlooking at all our individual relations with the Holy Spirit, for that is a wonderful thing, and a very real thing—and I believe it is open to us to prove the comfort of the Holy Spirit every day of our lives; I might say, every hour of the day. We can thus prove individually the comfort that the Holy Spirit would afford us.

But then, when we think of our assembly relations, think in the main it would be right to say that the comfort of the Holy Spirit is conveyed to us in ministry. That is another reason why we should be so thankful for the liberation amongst us of the ministry. It brings in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

I want to illustrate that from the account we have in 2 Chronicles of Asa’s reign. Asa was a good man, a very good man. We are told that “Asa’s heart was perfect all his days” (2 Chronicles 15: 17). At the end of his time he had a disease in his feet, but the Spirit of God comments that his heart was perfect towards God all his days.

Now the account of Asa’s reign begins by telling us that God gave him rest. It is a very remarkable thing that in his time they were free from war. It says that Asa did what was good; he took away the altars and the strange gods; he removed idolatry from Judah and he turned the hearts of the people to God. It says that the land had rest and they were without war for ten years. I think there is a link between that and the scripture that we read in Acts 9, that the assemblies had peace. In Asa’s reign there were ten years with no war, and the land had rest.

Well, what is Asa going to do? Is it a time of inaction with him? It certainly was not. And it is not to be a time of inactivity with us either. If God has given a time of peace and rest, there is work to be done. It is to be a time of action. So during this time of peace Asa says to Judah,

“Let us build these cities, and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars, while the land is yet before us; for we have sought Jehovah our God; we have sought him, and he has given us rest on every side. And they built and prospered” (2 Chronicles 14: 7).
It is the idea of what is constructive. God is giving Asa and the people with him an opportunity to build up the position and to strengthen it. Asa says, “Let us build these cities”.

I believe the local assemblies of the saints are very precious at the present time in the eyes of God. We want to see what these cities are to God. Asa says, ‘Let us build them up’. Dear brethren, let us occupy the time God is giving to us. If we are in a time of peace—and we are, in measure at least—if God gives us a time of rest, it is to be a time of construction. Let us be on that line. Asa is not looking backward; he is not bemoaning the time that was lost before he became king; what Asa is doing is building up these cities. They mean so much to God; it is the fortifying of the position, and the strengthening of it, because, sure enough, sooner or later the enemy will come up against it.

Now Asa did not only fortify the cities, he also had an army, and he equipped it with armour (2 Chronicles 14: 8). The panoply of God, in figure, was there. He had this army, ready to go out and do conflict with any adversary. It was not long before this king of Ethiopia, Zerah, came out against him with a thousand thousand. Think of an army like that! It would appear overwhelming. Even by present-day calculations it is an overwhelming host. Zerah, the Ethiopian, came against Asa with that, and Asa had to meet him with about half the number.

But he met him, dear brethren, in the fear of God, and he met him in the name of Jehovah. It says, “And Asa cried unto Jehovah his God, and said, Jehovah, it maketh no difference to thee to help, whether there be much or no power—help us, O Jehovah our God, for we rely on thee, and in thy name have we come against this multitude. Jehovah, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee” (2 Chronicles 14: 11). If you look at the note to “man” you will find that it refers to Enosh; frail, mortal man. That is what man is, frail and mortal. And if you multiply that by a million it is still frail, mortal man. So Asa says, “Let not man prevail against thee”.

What does it matter what their numbers are? Multiply them by any figure you like and it is still frail, mortal man. And Asa is crying to God about it, and God comes in and scatters the Ethiopians so that not one of them is left—not one of the million men; they are all destroyed.

It was the intervention of God, and the victory was complete. I tell you, dear brethren, I feel it myself, that we are to be prepared for great things. There is no limit to what God can do. I think we have to strengthen ourselves in our faith, and strengthen ourselves in our localities, and see what God can do for us. Asa did that. He strengthened those cities; he built up his army, and God acted for him.

What I want to come to is this, that, after the victory, it says in chapter 15: 1, “And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded. And he went out to meet Asa, and said to him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; Jehovah is with you while ye are with him; and if ye seek him he will be found of you, but if ye forsake him he will forsake you”. Now, dear brethren, I believe, subject to correction, that that is the way the comfort of the Holy Spirit comes in. You think of this prophet; it says that the Spirit of God came upon him, and he went out to meet Asa coming back from his victory. It reminds us immediately of Melchisedec going out to meet Abraham returning from his victory. The point of victory is a very dangerous one, because the enemy can very soon, and very easily, get an advantage.

The Spirit of God comes upon this prophet and he goes out to meet Asa. Now, he says, you listen to me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin. God is with you as you are with Him. Is not that a word for us? Is it not a word from the Holy Spirit? Would it not contain the comfort of the Holy Spirit? Asa had said, “We have sought Jehovah our God... and he has given us rest” (2 Chronicles 14: 7), and now the Holy Spirit is coming in—“Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin—Jehovah is with you while ye are with him”.

Well, dear brethren, if we do not get anything else today, let us get that! It is the word of the prophet, and we ought soberly to thank God for what comes to us in our localities through the prophetic ministry. I am sure that the Lord is speaking to us in more ways than one, and the prophetic ministry is going on. Let us humbly thank God for it. And the word is that God will be with us as we are with Him. What a word that is! Now I think that is the comfort of the Holy Spirit. It comes in this way.

So this prophet goes on. He tells Asa, going over the history, of a period when Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest. O, dear brethren, we have known conditions like that; when our relations with the true God were not what they ought to have been, and we were without the teaching priest. Our young ones have missed the teaching; the priestly teaching that is so necessary to build the saints up. Azariah reminds Asa of all that. But, he says, now He has given you rest; God has answered you, and “Jehovah is with you while ye are with him”.

The result of this is that Asa and all those with him, Judah and Benjamin, come together at Jerusalem and commit themselves in a full and whole-hearted way to God on the principle of an oath. They commit themselves irrevocably to the defence of what is for God. Well, that is, I believe, what the comfort of the Holy Spirit would result in as we experience it—and one would trust that there is some element of comfort entering into the meetings today. What are these meetings if they are not in line with what the Holy Spirit is doing? What we are learning, dear brethren, is not to trust in the flesh; not to trust in any ability that we may think we have, but to cast ourselves upon the Spirit of God, and see that, along with the fear of God that is to characterise the saints, there is this wonderful feature of the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

That is about all I have to say. I think it will be seen what I am aiming at. I think we ought to appreciate more fully the way that the ministry has been released among us—an authoritative ministry. This prophet is not speaking out of any position of weakness. He is speaking as the representative of God, and he has moral power. He says, “Jehovah is with you while ye are with him ... but if ye forsake him he will forsake you”. The word of authority is in it, and God is looking for subjection on the part of us all—not just on the part of some, but on the part of us all.

It is a remarkable thing, too, and this is perhaps what led me to think this way, that in the end of the epistle to the Romans Paul asks for the prayers of the saints. He says, “But I beseech you, brethren, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in prayers for me to God; that I may be saved from those that do not believe in Judaea; and that my ministry which I have for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints (Romans 15: 30, 31). You can see how the apostle in that passage is connecting the love of the Spirit with the ministry that God had given him for the saints, and the prayers of the saints are to be that the ministry may be acceptable.

Well, dear brethren, I trust there is something in this for us, as to the comfort of the Holy Spirit. I believe the time has come for it. We are in the last days, remnant times maybe publicly, and the comfort of the Holy Spirit is something that we are to experience increasingly amongst us.
May it be so, for His name’s sake!

Here is the seal written on both sides as it were, “the Lord knoweth them that are his”. How many of us carry this seal about? It was in the power of it that the great revival came about from which we are all benefiting now, and it remains. “The Lord knoweth them that are his”.

There is not one of them in the whole world who is not perfectly known to Christ; and if the Lord know those that are His. He never withdraws His eyes from one of them ... Then the other side is, “Let every one who names the name of the Lord withdraw from iniquity”. We have this seal in our possession on moral grounds—the power of representation. Although God is falsified on every hand, there is in those who hold the seal and act on it, a representation of God, and it means deliverance, for a true witness delivereth souls. There is no other way out, it is divinely appointed representation of God, in a day of general departure. He has opened up the way, and so the Lord says, “I have set before thee an opened door”—not an open one, but an opened one; the Lord has done it. He has the key of David; as He says, He opens and no one shuts, and He shuts and no one opens; and so “I have set before thee an opened door”. How it became opened I think is explained by the seal. We have the way opened for what I may call a little bit of collective representation. I think the Lord has great delight in the return to the collective thought; hence He says, “I have set before thee an opened door, and no man can shut it”. So that there is a way open to us, dear friends, a door opened by the Lord in which we, having a little strength as He says, may represent Him.

He says, thou “hast kept my word (it is in that that representation lies) and hast not denied my name”. How can those who take on another name represent Christ? It is misrepresentation; whereas this church—Philadelphia—affording a green spot for Christ, had not misrepresented Him; she had kept the word of His patience, and not denied His name.

She had a little power. The Lord appreciates a little collective power, and I think the fact that He does so should be treasured in the keenest way by us. There is no pretension attached to it; it is what the Lord sees and treasures. No misrepresentation; she keeps the word of His patience and does not deny His name.
J. Taylor, New Series Vol. 20, pp. 79–81
